title: RainGuru
name: rainguru
excerpt: RainGuru is an operational rainfall nowcasting system developed by TU Delft and HKV, using deep learning architectures like TrajGRU and ConvLSTM. It provides short-term precipitation forecasts based on radar and satellite data for flood early warning applications.
content: RainGuru leverages advanced deep learning techniques including Trajectory Gated Recurrent Units (TrajGRU) and Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) networks to deliver real-time rainfall nowcasting. Developed collaboratively by TU Delft and HKV, the system processes radar and satellite data to generate high-resolution precipitation forecasts up to several hours ahead. The tool is operationally deployed and supports flood early warning systems in the Netherlands and other regions. As highlighted in the UNESCO 2025 report on AI for Water Management, RainGuru represents a mature application of AI for hydrometeorological prediction. The system demonstrates how deep learning can outperform traditional extrapolation-based nowcasting methods, particularly for convective rainfall events. Its operational status (TRL 9) makes it one of the most advanced AI-based nowcasting tools currently available.
limitations: Limited to short lead times (0-6 hours). Performance degrades for stratiform rainfall. Requires high-quality radar data coverage which limits applicability in data-sparse regions.

title: IceNet
name: icenet
excerpt: IceNet is a deep learning sea ice forecasting system developed by the British Antarctic Survey and University of Cambridge. It uses a U-Net architecture to predict Arctic sea ice concentration months ahead, outperforming traditional dynamical models.
content: IceNet applies a probabilistic U-Net deep learning architecture to forecast Arctic sea ice extent at seasonal timescales. Developed by researchers at the British Antarctic Survey and the University of Cambridge, the system was trained on decades of satellite observations and climate model outputs. According to the UNESCO 2025 report, IceNet demonstrates how AI can provide skilful seasonal predictions of sea ice, which is critical for understanding cryosphere changes under global warming. The model produces ensemble-based probabilistic forecasts, enabling uncertainty quantification that is essential for decision-making. IceNet has shown skill improvements over leading physics-based models like ECMWF SEAS5 for lead times of 2-6 months. The tool is open-source and represents a significant advance in applying AI to cryosphere assessment and climate adaptation research.
developer_organization: British Antarctic Survey / University of Cambridge
limitations: Focused primarily on Arctic sea ice; Antarctic applications are less validated. Seasonal predictions still carry substantial uncertainty. Dependent on quality and continuity of satellite observation records.

title: GloFAS
name: glofas
excerpt: The Global Flood Awareness System (GloFAS) is an operational global flood forecasting system developed by ECMWF and the European Commission. It combines machine learning with physics-based hydrological models to provide medium-range flood predictions worldwide.
content: GloFAS (Global Flood Awareness System) is a cornerstone of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service, jointly developed by ECMWF and the European Commission's Joint Research Centre. The system integrates machine learning techniques with physics-based hydrological modelling to produce global river discharge forecasts at medium-range timescales. As documented in the UNESCO 2025 report on AI for Water Management, GloFAS provides probabilistic flood forecasts for major river basins worldwide, supporting disaster preparedness and humanitarian response. The system ingests numerical weather prediction outputs and runs them through calibrated hydrological models enhanced with ML-based post-processing. GloFAS is fully operational (TRL 9) and provides daily updated forecasts accessible through a web interface. It serves as a critical tool for international organizations and national agencies in flood-prone regions with limited local forecasting capacity.
limitations: Spatial resolution may be insufficient for small catchments. Performance varies significantly across regions depending on calibration data availability. Limited skill in flash flood prediction due to medium-range temporal focus.

title: GraphCast
name: graphcast
excerpt: GraphCast is a Graph Neural Network-based weather forecasting model developed by Google DeepMind. It produces 10-day global weather forecasts in under a minute, matching or outperforming traditional numerical weather prediction models.
content: GraphCast represents a paradigm shift in weather forecasting, using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to learn atmospheric dynamics directly from ERA5 reanalysis data. Developed by Google DeepMind, the model can generate 10-day global forecasts at 0.25° resolution in under 60 seconds on a single TPU, compared to hours of supercomputer time for traditional NWP models. The UNESCO 2025 report highlights GraphCast as a landmark achievement, demonstrating that AI can match the accuracy of the gold-standard HRES model from ECMWF across most variables. The model processes atmospheric variables on a multi-mesh graph structure that preserves spatial relationships at multiple scales. GraphCast has been released as open-source, enabling the broader research community to build upon its architecture. Its operational potential is being explored by weather agencies worldwide for integration into ensemble forecasting workflows.
limitations: Requires high-quality initial conditions from traditional NWP systems. Limited ability to predict extreme events outside training distribution. Cannot currently assimilate observations directly; depends on data assimilation from conventional systems.

title: Pangu-Weather
name: pangu-weather
excerpt: Pangu-Weather is a 3D Transformer-based deep learning model developed by Huawei Cloud for global weather forecasting. It processes atmospheric data across multiple pressure levels, offering competitive accuracy with traditional numerical weather prediction at dramatically lower computational cost.
content: Pangu-Weather employs a novel 3D Earth-Specific Transformer architecture to capture complex atmospheric dynamics across multiple pressure levels simultaneously. Developed by Huawei Cloud, it was one of the first AI models to demonstrate competitive performance against ECMWF's HRES operational forecasts for medium-range weather prediction. The UNESCO 2025 report identifies Pangu-Weather as a key milestone in the AI weather forecasting revolution, showcasing how deep learning can process the three-dimensional structure of the atmosphere. The model was trained on 39 years of ERA5 reanalysis data and can generate 7-day global forecasts in seconds. Its hierarchical temporal aggregation strategy allows efficient multi-step forecasting without excessive error accumulation. Pangu-Weather's architecture has influenced subsequent AI weather models and contributed to advancing the field of data-driven earth system modelling.
limitations: Still relies on ERA5 initial conditions produced by traditional data assimilation systems. Uncertainty quantification is limited compared to ensemble NWP approaches. Extreme weather events at the tails of the distribution remain challenging.

title: FourCastNet
name: fourcastnet
excerpt: FourCastNet is NVIDIA's deep learning weather model based on Adaptive Fourier Neural Operators (AFNO). It generates global weather forecasts at high resolution and enables rapid generation of large forecast ensembles for uncertainty quantification.
content: FourCastNet (Fourier ForeCasting Neural Network) introduces Adaptive Fourier Neural Operators to weather prediction, enabling efficient learning of atmospheric dynamics in spectral space. Developed by NVIDIA, the model operates on a 0.25° global grid and can produce week-ahead forecasts at unprecedented speed, allowing the generation of thousands of ensemble members for probabilistic forecasting. The UNESCO 2025 report highlights FourCastNet as an innovative approach that leverages the mathematical properties of Fourier transforms to efficiently handle global-scale atmospheric patterns. The model was trained on ERA5 reanalysis data and has demonstrated particular skill in forecasting large-scale atmospheric circulation patterns. Its ensemble generation capability is especially valuable for extreme event prediction and risk assessment. FourCastNet's open-source release through NVIDIA's Earth-2 platform has made it accessible for research and operational experimentation.
limitations: Forecast skill deteriorates faster than physics-based models at longer lead times. Spectral approach may smooth out small-scale features. Dependent on initial conditions from traditional NWP data assimilation.

title: AIFS
name: aifs
excerpt: AIFS (Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System) is ECMWF's machine learning-enhanced weather prediction system. It integrates AI models into ECMWF's operational forecasting pipeline, combining the strengths of data-driven and physics-based approaches.
content: AIFS represents ECMWF's strategic effort to integrate machine learning into its world-leading operational weather forecasting infrastructure. The system enhances traditional numerical weather prediction with ML-based components for improved post-processing, downscaling, and forecast initialization. As described in the UNESCO 2025 report, AIFS is designed to operate alongside ECMWF's existing IFS (Integrated Forecasting System), leveraging decades of meteorological expertise while harnessing the computational efficiency of AI. The system uses data from ECMWF's extensive network of weather models and global gauging stations. AIFS is in advanced development (TRL 7-8) with components already being tested in semi-operational settings. It represents a pragmatic approach to AI integration in weather services, where reliability and continuity of service are paramount.
limitations: Still under active development with components at various maturity levels. Full integration with operational IFS pipeline requires extensive validation. Performance benchmarks against standalone AI models are still being established.

title: AIDSII
name: aidsii
excerpt: AIDSII (AI-Driven Smart Irrigation Infrastructure) combines CNN-LSTM deep learning with IoT sensor networks for precision agriculture water management. The system optimizes irrigation scheduling based on real-time soil moisture, weather, and crop health data.
content: AIDSII integrates Convolutional Neural Networks with Long Short-Term Memory architectures (CNN-LSTM) and Internet of Things sensor networks to create an intelligent irrigation management system. The prototype system collects real-time data from soil moisture sensors, weather stations, and satellite imagery to predict crop water requirements and optimize irrigation scheduling. As highlighted in the UNESCO 2025 report, AIDSII exemplifies how AI can address the water-food nexus by reducing agricultural water consumption while maintaining or improving crop yields. The system's deep learning components process both spatial (satellite imagery) and temporal (sensor time series) data to capture complex soil-plant-atmosphere interactions. Currently at prototype stage (TRL 4-6), AIDSII has been validated in pilot agricultural sites demonstrating significant water savings. The integration of edge computing with IoT sensors enables near real-time decision support for farmers.
limitations: Requires dense IoT sensor deployment which increases infrastructure costs. Model transferability to different crops and climatic zones is not yet validated. Connectivity and power requirements limit deployment in remote agricultural areas.

title: COALA
name: coala
excerpt: COALA is an EU-funded project that applies AI to Copernicus Earth observation data for precision agriculture and irrigation monitoring. It provides seasonal crop water demand forecasts and irrigation optimization at regional scale.
content: COALA (Copernicus for Agriculture in Africa and Latin America) leverages artificial intelligence applied to Copernicus satellite data and Earth observation products for agricultural water management at regional scale. The project, funded by the European Union, develops AI-based services for crop monitoring, irrigation scheduling, and water productivity assessment. The UNESCO 2025 report identifies COALA as a significant initiative bridging the gap between satellite-based Earth observation and actionable agricultural water management decisions. The system processes multi-spectral satellite imagery to estimate evapotranspiration, soil moisture, and crop health indicators at field scale. At TRL 7-8, COALA services are being operationally tested in multiple countries across Africa and Latin America. The project demonstrates how AI can democratize access to precision agriculture technologies in developing regions through freely available satellite data.
limitations: Cloud cover frequently limits optical satellite data availability in tropical regions. Spatial resolution may be insufficient for smallholder farming systems. Ground truth validation data is sparse in target deployment regions.

title: NEXOGENESIS
name: nexogenesis
excerpt: NEXOGENESIS is an EU Horizon project involving 20 partners that applies reinforcement learning to optimize Water-Energy-Food nexus management. It develops decision-support tools for long-term sustainable resource allocation at catchment scale.
content: NEXOGENESIS addresses the complex interdependencies between water, energy, and food systems using advanced reinforcement learning algorithms to find optimal resource allocation strategies. This large-scale EU Horizon project, involving 20 institutional partners, develops AI-driven decision-support tools for policymakers managing interconnected resource systems. As documented in the UNESCO 2025 report, NEXOGENESIS represents a frontier application of AI for understanding and managing the Water-Energy-Food (WEF) nexus under climate change scenarios. The reinforcement learning approach enables the system to explore vast decision spaces and identify strategies that balance competing demands across sectors. Currently at research stage (TRL 1-3), the project is developing and testing its framework across multiple European catchments with different nexus characteristics. The long-term temporal scale reflects the tool's focus on strategic planning and policy evaluation rather than operational management.
limitations: Complex multi-objective optimization may produce solutions that are difficult for policymakers to interpret. Data integration across water, energy, and food sectors remains challenging. Results are highly sensitive to assumptions about future climate and socioeconomic scenarios.

title: XFLEX HYDRO
name: xflex-hydro
excerpt: XFLEX HYDRO is an EU-funded project that uses artificial neural networks and machine learning to optimize hydropower generation flexibility. It develops AI tools for improving the efficiency and responsiveness of hydropower plants to grid demands.
content: XFLEX HYDRO applies artificial neural networks (ANN) and machine learning techniques to enhance the operational flexibility of hydropower plants, enabling them to better respond to variable renewable energy integration in electricity grids. The EU-funded project develops predictive models for turbine performance, reservoir inflow forecasting, and optimal dispatch scheduling. According to the UNESCO 2025 report, XFLEX HYDRO addresses the critical role of hydropower as a flexible energy storage and generation technology in the transition to renewable energy systems. The AI components process data from gauging stations and IoT sensors installed at pilot hydropower facilities to predict short-term inflow and optimize turbine operations. At prototype stage (TRL 4-6), the system has been tested at several European hydropower plants demonstrating improved efficiency and responsiveness. The project contributes to both water resources management and energy system optimization within the broader WEF nexus context.
limitations: Optimization models are calibrated for specific hydropower plant configurations and may not transfer easily. Balancing environmental flow requirements with grid flexibility objectives remains challenging. Integration with existing SCADA systems at aging hydropower facilities presents technical barriers.

title: SAM (Segment Anything Model)
name: sam-segment-anything
excerpt: Meta AI's Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a foundation model for zero-shot image segmentation being applied to flood mapping and water body delineation from satellite imagery. Its ability to segment objects without task-specific training makes it highly versatile for remote sensing applications.
content: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) developed by Meta AI is a zero-shot computer vision foundation model that can segment any object in an image without prior task-specific training. In the water sector, researchers are applying SAM to flood extent mapping, water body delineation, and damage assessment from satellite and aerial imagery. The UNESCO 2025 report identifies SAM as a transformative foundation model with significant potential for water-related remote sensing applications. Its zero-shot capability means it can be deployed rapidly during flood events without requiring labelled training data specific to the disaster area. The model processes satellite imagery and Earth observation data to produce pixel-level segmentation maps that can be used for near real-time flood monitoring. Currently at research stage (TRL 4-6) for water applications, SAM represents the growing trend of adapting large foundation models for domain-specific environmental monitoring tasks.
limitations: Not specifically trained for water/flood segmentation, requiring prompt engineering or fine-tuning for optimal results. Performance on SAR imagery (critical for cloudy conditions) is less validated. Computational requirements may limit real-time deployment in resource-constrained settings.

title: CLIP
name: clip
excerpt: OpenAI's CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) is a multimodal foundation model being explored for zero-shot water infrastructure damage assessment. It can classify and describe flood damage from images using natural language prompts without task-specific training.
content: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) by OpenAI is a multimodal AI model that learns visual concepts from natural language supervision, enabling zero-shot image classification and retrieval. In the water domain, researchers are exploring CLIP for rapid assessment of water infrastructure damage, flood impact classification, and post-disaster reconnaissance from aerial and satellite imagery. The UNESCO 2025 report notes CLIP's potential as a foundation model for water-related applications where labelled training data is scarce or unavailable during emergencies. By describing damage categories in natural language, responders can use CLIP to automatically classify images of flood-affected infrastructure without pre-training on specific disaster datasets. The model's ability to process both visual and textual information makes it particularly useful for integrating social media imagery with formal assessment workflows. Currently at early research stage (TRL 1-3) for water applications, CLIP represents the frontier of multimodal AI for disaster response.
limitations: Not specifically designed for remote sensing or water infrastructure; domain adaptation is needed. Zero-shot performance may be insufficient for fine-grained damage classification. Potential biases from web-scraped training data may affect performance in diverse geographic contexts.

title: DeepONet
name: deeponet
excerpt: DeepONet (Deep Operator Network) is a neural network architecture for learning nonlinear operators, applied to groundwater flow emulation. It enables fast approximation of partial differential equation solutions for subsurface hydrology modelling.
content: DeepONet is a deep learning architecture designed to learn continuous nonlinear operators, enabling it to approximate solutions of partial differential equations governing groundwater flow and transport. Developed by various research groups building on foundational work by Lu et al., DeepONet uses a branch-trunk network structure to map input functions (boundary conditions, parameters) to output functions (pressure heads, concentration fields). The UNESCO 2025 report highlights DeepONet as a promising approach to creating fast surrogate models (emulators) for computationally expensive groundwater simulations. Once trained, DeepONet can produce predictions orders of magnitude faster than traditional numerical solvers, making it valuable for uncertainty quantification and optimization workflows. The architecture's ability to handle variable input parameterizations makes it particularly suited for groundwater inverse problems. At research stage (TRL 1-3), DeepONet for groundwater applications is an active area of investigation with growing published literature.
limitations: Accuracy depends heavily on the quality and diversity of training simulations. Generalization to geological settings not represented in training data is uncertain. Physical consistency of predictions is not guaranteed without additional constraints.

title: Google Flood Hub
name: google-flood-hub
excerpt: Google Flood Hub is an operational AI-powered flood forecasting platform that provides riverine flood predictions for developing countries. It combines machine learning with satellite imagery and gauging station data to deliver actionable flood warnings at national scale.
content: Google Flood Hub is an operational flood forecasting platform that applies machine learning and remote sensing technologies to provide flood warnings in regions with limited hydrometeorological infrastructure. The platform integrates satellite imagery, gauging station data, and weather model outputs through ML algorithms to generate river level predictions and flood inundation maps. As emphasized in the UNESCO 2025 report, Google Flood Hub represents a landmark effort to democratize access to advanced flood forecasting capabilities in developing countries across Asia and Africa. The system has been deployed in India, Bangladesh, and numerous other countries, providing forecasts with lead times sufficient for evacuation and emergency preparedness. At full operational maturity (TRL 9), the platform serves millions of people through integration with Google Search and Google Maps. Google Flood Hub demonstrates how big tech investment in AI for humanitarian applications can address critical gaps in global flood early warning coverage.
limitations: Coverage is still expanding and does not yet include all flood-prone regions. Model accuracy varies by region and is lower where gauging data is sparse. Flood inundation mapping resolution may be insufficient for urban areas with complex topography.

title: FIER
name: fier
excerpt: FIER (Flood Inundation Extent from Remote sensing) uses machine learning with Rotated Empirical Orthogonal Function analysis to estimate flood extent from satellite observations. It provides rapid flood mapping capabilities for disaster response and impact assessment.
content: FIER (Flood Inundation Extent from Remote sensing) applies machine learning techniques combined with Rotated Empirical Orthogonal Function (REOF) analysis to extract flood inundation extent from satellite observations. The system processes multi-temporal satellite imagery and Earth observation data to generate flood maps that can support disaster response and recovery planning. The UNESCO 2025 report identifies FIER as an innovative approach that combines statistical dimensionality reduction with machine learning for improved flood extent estimation. The REOF technique captures dominant spatial patterns of water surface variability, which ML algorithms then classify into flood and non-flood areas. At research stage (TRL 4-6), FIER has been validated across multiple flood events demonstrating promising accuracy compared to manual mapping approaches. The system's ability to work with freely available satellite data makes it particularly relevant for applications in resource-constrained settings.
limitations: Optical satellite data is unavailable during cloudy conditions typical of flood events. Temporal resolution of satellite revisits may miss peak flood extent. Accuracy is reduced in urban and vegetated areas where water surface detection is more challenging.

title: SWMM + AI
name: swmm-ai
excerpt: SWMM + AI combines the EPA's Storm Water Management Model with machine learning techniques for enhanced urban stormwater and drainage modelling. The hybrid approach improves prediction accuracy and computational efficiency for real-time urban flood management.
content: SWMM + AI represents the integration of machine learning techniques with the EPA's well-established Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) for improved urban stormwater and drainage system modelling. This hybrid approach combines the physical process understanding embedded in SWMM with data-driven ML methods for enhanced calibration, real-time updating, and surrogate modelling. As discussed in the UNESCO 2025 report, the combination of physics-based and AI approaches is particularly effective for urban drainage systems where complex infrastructure interactions are difficult to model purely from data. The system leverages IoT sensors, radar data, and gauging stations to provide real-time state estimation and short-term flood predictions for urban catchments. At production readiness (TRL 7-8), various SWMM + AI implementations are being used by water utilities and municipalities for operational flood management. The open-source nature of SWMM facilitates integration of ML components by the research and practitioner community.
limitations: Urban drainage model setup requires detailed sewer network data which is often outdated or unavailable. ML components need retraining when infrastructure changes occur. Real-time sensor data quality issues can propagate through the hybrid modelling chain.

title: PINNs for Hydrology
name: pinns-hydrology
excerpt: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) embed physical laws as constraints within neural network training for groundwater and hydrological modelling. This approach ensures physically consistent predictions while leveraging the flexibility of deep learning.
content: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) represent a paradigm that embeds governing physical equations—such as the Richards equation for unsaturated flow or Darcy's law for groundwater—directly into the neural network loss function during training. Developed by various research groups building on foundational work by Raissi et al., PINNs for hydrology ensure that predictions respect known physical laws while learning from observational data. The UNESCO 2025 report highlights PINNs as a promising approach to address the data scarcity challenge in hydrological modelling by incorporating prior physical knowledge as a regularization mechanism. This physics-constrained approach is particularly valuable for groundwater modelling where observation data is sparse and expensive to obtain. PINNs can solve both forward problems (predicting system behaviour) and inverse problems (estimating parameters from observations) within a unified framework. At early research stage (TRL 1-3), PINNs for hydrology are an active and rapidly growing research area with potential applications across multiple water management domains.
limitations: Training convergence can be difficult for complex multi-physics problems. Scaling to large spatial domains with heterogeneous properties remains challenging. Computational cost during training may negate speed advantages over traditional solvers for simple cases.

title: NeuralGCM
name: neuralgcm
excerpt: NeuralGCM is a hybrid model from Google and Caltech that integrates machine learning with General Circulation Models for climate change modelling. It combines the physical fidelity of GCMs with ML-based parameterizations of sub-grid processes.
content: NeuralGCM (Neural General Circulation Model) is a groundbreaking hybrid approach that integrates machine learning components within the framework of traditional General Circulation Models (GCMs) for improved climate and weather simulation. Developed collaboratively by Google Research and Caltech, NeuralGCM replaces computationally expensive sub-grid parameterizations in GCMs with learned neural network approximations while preserving the physical dynamics core. The UNESCO 2025 report highlights NeuralGCM as a significant advance toward next-generation climate models that combine physical understanding with data-driven learning. The hybrid architecture maintains conservation laws and other physical constraints while improving the representation of processes like convection and cloud formation. NeuralGCM has demonstrated competitive or superior performance compared to both traditional GCMs and pure AI weather models across multiple metrics. At research stage (TRL 4-6), the model points toward a future where climate projections benefit from both accumulated physical understanding and machine learning capabilities.
limitations: Long-term climate projection stability beyond training data period is not yet fully validated. Learned parameterizations may not generalize well to climate regimes not represented in historical data. Interaction between ML and physics components can introduce subtle numerical instabilities.

title: GenCast
name: gencast
excerpt: GenCast is a diffusion model-based probabilistic weather forecasting system developed by Google DeepMind. It generates calibrated ensemble forecasts that outperform traditional NWP ensembles for medium-range weather prediction.
content: GenCast applies diffusion models—a class of generative AI—to produce probabilistic ensemble weather forecasts with calibrated uncertainty estimates. Developed by Google DeepMind, the system generates diverse and physically plausible weather scenarios by learning the conditional distribution of future atmospheric states given current observations. The UNESCO 2025 report identifies GenCast as a notable advance in applying generative AI techniques to weather prediction, addressing a key limitation of earlier deterministic AI weather models. Unlike deterministic approaches, GenCast naturally captures forecast uncertainty by generating multiple plausible future states, which is essential for risk-based decision-making in water management. The diffusion model architecture enables generation of spatially coherent ensemble members that respect the multivariate correlation structure of atmospheric variables. At research stage (TRL 4-6), GenCast demonstrates the growing role of generative models in advancing the state of the art in probabilistic weather forecasting.
limitations: Diffusion sampling is computationally more expensive than single-pass deterministic models. Extreme event frequencies in generated ensembles need careful validation. Dependent on ERA5 reanalysis for training, inheriting any biases present in the reanalysis product.

title: Wuqiangxi AI System
name: wuqiangxi-ai-system
excerpt: The Wuqiangxi AI System is an operational dam monitoring platform developed by SPIC (State Power Investment Corporation) that uses computer vision and drone-based inspection for hydropower infrastructure safety. It represents one of the most mature AI deployments for dam monitoring worldwide.
content: The Wuqiangxi AI System is an advanced operational platform for hydropower dam monitoring and safety assessment, deployed at the Wuqiangxi Dam in China by the State Power Investment Corporation (SPIC). The system integrates computer vision algorithms with drone-based inspection capabilities and IoT sensor networks to provide continuous monitoring of dam structural integrity and environmental conditions. As highlighted in the UNESCO 2025 report, the Wuqiangxi system exemplifies how AI can enhance critical water infrastructure safety through automated anomaly detection and predictive maintenance. Computer vision models analyze drone imagery and fixed camera feeds to detect surface cracks, seepage, and other structural anomalies that may indicate developing problems. The system also processes satellite imagery for broader environmental monitoring of the reservoir and surrounding terrain. At full operational maturity (TRL 9), the Wuqiangxi AI System is one of the world's most advanced examples of AI applied to dam safety, though its proprietary nature limits broader adoption.
limitations: Proprietary system with limited transferability to other dam types and configurations. Computer vision models trained on specific dam characteristics may not generalize. Regulatory and data-sharing restrictions limit independent validation of system performance.

title: ConvLSTM/TrajGRU
name: convlstm-trajgru
excerpt: ConvLSTM and TrajGRU are foundational deep learning architectures developed by the academic community for rainfall nowcasting from radar sequences. These recurrent convolutional networks form the basis of many operational precipitation nowcasting systems worldwide.
content: Convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) and Trajectory GRU (TrajGRU) are pioneering deep learning architectures that combine recurrent neural network temporal modelling with convolutional spatial processing for precipitation nowcasting. Originally developed by academic researchers, these architectures learn to extrapolate radar echo sequences to predict short-term rainfall evolution. The UNESCO 2025 report recognizes ConvLSTM and TrajGRU as foundational contributions to AI-based precipitation nowcasting, having inspired numerous subsequent models and operational implementations worldwide. ConvLSTM extends the standard LSTM architecture to process spatiotemporal sequences, while TrajGRU introduces trajectory-based connections that better capture the advective motion of weather systems. These models are typically trained on historical radar data and can be enhanced with satellite imagery for improved performance. At research-to-prototype stage (TRL 4-6), many variations of these architectures have been developed and some have been incorporated into operational nowcasting systems like RainGuru.
limitations: Prediction quality decreases rapidly beyond 1-2 hours lead time. Tend to produce blurry predictions at longer lead times due to averaging over possible futures. Performance varies significantly depending on radar data quality and rainfall type.
